title: Developmental anatomy — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: Obeng's HB2 embryology lectures (F. K. Addai, SMD KNUST)

questions.stem: The complete process of spermatogenesis, from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Spermatogenesis takes ~64 days: spermatocytogenesis (16) + meiosis (24) + spermiogenesis (24).

questions.stem: Spermiogenesis, the cytodifferentiation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon, takes about
questions.why: Spermiogenesis (tail, acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, shedding of cytoplasm) takes ~24 days.

questions.stem: The blood-testis barrier, formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells, separates a basal compartment (spermatogonia, mitosis) from an adluminal compartment where
questions.why: The adluminal compartment houses spermatocytes undergoing meiosis, shielded from the immune system by the barrier.

questions.stem: Meiosis in the male occurs only after puberty, which is important because meiotic products
questions.why: Meiotic cells carry novel antigens; the blood-testis barrier plus post-pubertal timing (mature immune system) prevents autoimmune destruction and infertility.

questions.stem: The reserve stem cell of the spermatogenic lineage that can continue spermatogenesis throughout life is the
questions.why: The type A dark (Ad) spermatogonium is the reserve stem cell; type A pale divides to type B, which gives primary spermatocytes.

questions.stem: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division at which stage, from fetal life until puberty?
questions.why: Oocytes rest in the dictyotene (diffuse diplotene) stage of prophase I, held by oocyte maturation inhibitor until the LH surge.

questions.stem: Meiotic arrest of the primary oocyte is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor secreted by the
questions.why: Follicular (granulosa) cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), holding the oocyte in meiotic arrest.

questions.stem: A normal ejaculate volume is about
questions.why: Semen volume is ~1.8-5.5 ml (average ~3.5 ml), with about 100 million spermatozoa per ml.

questions.stem: For fertility, at least what fraction of spermatozoa should be motile with progressive forward movement?
questions.why: At least ~40% of sperm should be motile with forward progression; a minimum of ~15 million per ejaculate is needed.

questions.stem: Immotile sperm flagella due to a ciliary (dynein) defect, as in Kartagener's syndrome, is
questions.why: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener's) gives immotile flagella and infertility.

questions.stem: The term for a complete absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate, even after centrifugation, is
questions.why: Azoospermia is no sperm in the ejaculate; aspermia is absence of semen (no ejaculation).

questions.stem: During the acrosome reaction, the enzyme that digests the cumulus/corona cells around the oocyte is
questions.why: Hyaluronidase digests the corona radiata; acrosin (exposed on the inner acrosomal membrane) helps penetrate the zona; neuraminidase is also released.

questions.stem: Fertilization proceeds in three sequential steps: penetration of the corona radiata, penetration of the zona pellucida, and

options.label: C
options.text: fusion of the oocyte and sperm cell membranes

questions.why: The three steps are corona penetration, zona penetration, then membrane binding and fusion.

questions.stem: Polyspermic fertilization in the human characteristically

options.label: B
options.text: is the usual mechanism of twinning

options.label: D
options.text: dies at or after the 8-cell stage

questions.why: A polyspermic pre-embryo does not proceed beyond a few cleavages and dies around the 8-cell stage.

questions.stem: A hydatidiform mole, with masses of trophoblast secreting large amounts of hCG and no viable fetus, may arise from

options.label: C
options.text: arrest of the oocyte in dictyotene

questions.why: Loss of a pronucleus (often with polyspermic fertilization) gives molar pregnancy with excess trophoblast and hCG.

questions.stem: Cleavage of the human zygote is described as holoblastic, meaning the division furrows

options.label: A
options.text: pass completely through the whole cell

options.label: B
options.text: involve only part of the cell

questions.why: Human cleavage is holoblastic (complete) and occurs without growth, fractionating the zygote into smaller blastomeres.

questions.stem: The ball of blastomeres is moved from the oviduct to the uterus by peristalsis and by

options.label: B
options.text: a ciliary escalator of oviductal cilia

questions.why: Rhythmic beating of oviductal cilia (the 'ciliary escalator') plus tubal peristalsis move the conceptus to the uterus.

questions.stem: Compaction of the morula is driven mainly by
questions.why: E-cadherin tightens cell-cell contacts during compaction and outer-cell polarization precedes the first lineage decision.

questions.stem: The blastocoel cavity forms when outer trophoblast cells pump ions using
questions.why: Outer cells express Na+/K+-ATPase; the resulting osmotic influx of fluid forms the blastocoel, converting morula to blastocyst.

questions.stem: In the morula-to-blastocyst transition, trophoblast fate in the outer cells is promoted by the transcription factor
questions.why: In outer cells the Hippo pathway is inactive, YAP enters the nucleus and activates CDX2 for trophoblast fate; inner cells keep OCT4/SOX2/NANOG.

questions.stem: Pluripotency of the inner cell mass is maintained by the transcription factors
questions.why: OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG mutually reinforce pluripotency in the ICM and suppress trophoblast genes.

questions.stem: Implantation requires a receptive endometrium and a blastocyst that has

options.label: B
options.text: hatched out of the zona pellucida

questions.why: The blastocyst must hatch from the zona to expose the trophoblast to the receptive mid-secretory endometrium.

questions.stem: The three stages of implantation, in order, are
questions.why: Implantation proceeds as apposition, then adhesion, then trophoblast invasion through the epithelial basement membrane.

questions.stem: The usual site of implantation is the

options.label: E
options.text: lower uterine segment over the os

questions.why: Normal implantation is in the body of the uterus, upper posterior wall near the midline; elsewhere is ectopic.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-diamniotic (Mo-Di) monozygotic twins, sharing one placenta but with separate amnions, make up about
questions.why: Mo-Di is the commonest monozygotic pattern (~60-70%); sharing one placenta risks twin-to-twin transfusion.

questions.stem: Monochorionic-monoamniotic (Mo-Mo) twins, the riskiest type, carry a mortality of about
questions.why: Mo-Mo twins (~5% of twins) share one placenta and one amnion, with a mortality around 20%.

questions.stem: Conjoined twinning is possible only in which type of monozygotic twins?
questions.why: Conjoining results from late (post-bilaminar-disc) splitting and occurs only in Mo-Mo twins.

questions.stem: Conjoined twins joined at the cranium are termed
questions.why: Craniopagus (joined at the skull) accounts for about 2-6% of conjoined twins.

questions.stem: The simultaneous presence of two embryos conceived weeks apart in the same uterus is
questions.why: Superfetation is a second conception during an existing pregnancy; it is very rare and almost always linked to ART.

questions.stem: The syncytiotrophoblast differs from the cytotrophoblast in that it is

options.label: B
options.text: the stem layer for the cytotrophoblast

questions.why: The syncytiotrophoblast is multinucleated, amitotic, invasive, in contact with maternal blood, secretes hCG and performs most placental functions; the cytotrophoblast is its mitotic stem layer.

questions.stem: The primary (primitive) yolk sac is lined by a thin layer called
questions.why: Hypoblast-derived Heuser's (exocoelomic) membrane lines the former blastocyst cavity to form the primary yolk sac.

questions.stem: Extraembryonic somatic (parietal) mesoderm is associated with the amnion and chorion, whereas extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the
questions.why: Somatic extraembryonic mesoderm lines the cytotrophoblast and amnion (with ectoderm); splanchnic covers the yolk sac and allantois (with endoderm).

questions.stem: The umbilical cord develops from the
questions.why: The connecting (body) stalk of extraembryonic mesoderm that suspends the disc in the chorionic cavity becomes the umbilical cord.

questions.stem: The villous chorion related to the decidua basalis, forming the fetal placenta, is the
questions.why: Chorion frondosum (bushy chorion) faces the decidua basalis and forms the fetal placenta; chorion laeve (smooth) faces the capsularis and regresses.

questions.stem: The connective tissue of the umbilical cord that cushions its vessels is
questions.why: The cord vessels are embedded in Wharton's jelly, a mucous connective tissue from extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.stem: Early in development the umbilical cord contains two arteries and two veins; later there remains
questions.why: One umbilical vein degenerates, leaving the definitive cord with two arteries and one vein.

questions.stem: A chorionic villus becomes a tertiary villus when it acquires

options.label: B
options.text: blood vessels in its mesenchymal core

questions.why: Primary villi (trophoblast) gain a mesenchyme core (secondary), then blood vessels (tertiary), enabling exchange.

questions.stem: Villi that anchor the placenta to the decidua basalis are the
questions.why: Anchoring villi insert into the decidua; terminal (free) villi are the main sites of materno-fetal exchange.

questions.stem: In the mature (late) placenta, the number of layers separating maternal and fetal blood is
questions.why: The late barrier has three layers (syncytiotrophoblast, fused basement membranes, fetal capillary endothelium); the early barrier has six.

questions.stem: Placenta accreta is characterised by

options.label: B
options.text: the placenta overlying the internal os

questions.why: In accreta the decidua basalis is deficient so villi adhere abnormally; percreta is penetration through the myometrium; praevia overlies the os.

questions.stem: At term the normal amniotic fluid volume is about
questions.why: Amniotic fluid rises to ~800-1000 ml near term (it peaks ~1000 ml around 32-34 weeks).

questions.stem: From about 20 weeks to term, the main source of amniotic fluid is
questions.why: By term fetal kidneys make 600-700 ml urine/day (the chief source); lungs add ~250 ml/day; the fetus swallows ~500 ml/day.

questions.stem: After delivery, the placenta normally separates through the
questions.why: Placental separation occurs through the spongy layer of the decidua basalis, aided by a retroplacental haematoma.

questions.stem: The placental hormone with growth-hormone-like actions that promotes maternal lipolysis and glucose sparing is
questions.why: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin (human placental lactogen) has GH-like effects and promotes mammary development.

questions.stem: Gastrulation begins with the appearance of the primitive streak on the
questions.why: The primitive streak appears in the caudal (posterior) three-fifths of the epiblast around day 15-16.

questions.stem: Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak by a process called
questions.why: EMT (driven by Snail repressing E-cadherin, with FGF8/WNT) lets epiblast cells detach and migrate through the streak.

questions.stem: The master inducer (a TGF-beta family member) that initiates primitive-streak formation is
questions.why: NODAL induces the primitive streak; WNT3/beta-catenin and FGF8 reinforce streak formation and migration.

questions.stem: The first wave of cells migrating through the primitive streak displaces the hypoblast to become
questions.why: The first wave forms definitive endoderm (also replacing Heuser's membrane); the second wave forms mesoderm; epiblast left behind is ectoderm.

questions.stem: The notochord secretes which signalling molecule to pattern the neural tube and somites?
questions.why: The notochord secretes Sonic hedgehog, induces neuroectoderm (inhibiting BMP) and establishes the midline axis.

questions.stem: The two points where ectoderm and endoderm stay fused with no intervening mesoderm are the
questions.why: Mesoderm surrounds the disc except at the cranial oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) and caudal cloacal membranes.

questions.stem: The human embryo has a total of how many pairs of somites?
questions.why: There are 42-44 somites: 5 occipital, 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 8-10 coccygeal, appearing days 20-31.

questions.stem: The lateral plate mesoderm is split into somatic and splanchnic layers by the
questions.why: A cavity (the intraembryonic coelom) splits the lateral plate into somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) leaflets.

questions.stem: The embryonic period of organogenesis, when the embryo is most sensitive to teratogens, spans weeks
questions.why: Gastrulation begins the embryonic stage (weeks 3-8) of organogenesis, a period of high teratogen susceptibility.

questions.stem: Insufficient migration of mesoderm around the oropharyngeal membrane is associated with
questions.why: Deficient cranial mesoderm underlies holoprosencephaly (failure of forebrain cleavage); deficient caudal mesoderm gives sirenomelia.

questions.stem: Caudal dysgenesis with fused lower limbs (the 'mermaid' malformation) from insufficient caudal mesoderm is
questions.why: Sirenomelia (caudal dysgenesis) results from deficient mesoderm around the cloacal membrane.

questions.stem: Remnants of the primitive streak that persist can give rise, in the newborn, to a
questions.why: Failed degeneration of primitive-streak cells can produce a sacrococcygeal teratoma in the buttock region.

questions.stem: New blood vessels forming de novo from angioblasts that differentiate from mesenchyme is called
questions.why: Vasculogenesis forms the first vessels from angioblasts; angiogenesis is sprouting of capillaries from existing vessels.

questions.stem: The primordium of the heart first forms in the
questions.why: The heart primordium forms in the cardiogenic plate (primary heart field) at the cranial end of the embryo.

questions.stem: The single primitive heart tube forms by
questions.why: Two endocardial (heart) tubes move ventrally with folding and fuse into one primitive heart tube.

questions.stem: The cephalic (arterial) end of the bulbus cordis elongates to become the
questions.why: The cephalic bulbus cordis elongates into the truncus arteriosus; from cranial to caudal the tube is bulbus cordis, ventricle, atrium, sinus venosus.

questions.stem: To accommodate elongation, the heart tube bends from left to right forming the
questions.why: The tube folds right to form the bulboventricular (heart) loop.

questions.stem: The superior and inferior endocardial cushions fuse to partition the atrioventricular canal, forming the
questions.why: AV cushion fusion (septum intermedium) divides the AV canal into right and left channels.

questions.stem: The gap between the growing edge of the septum primum and the endocardial cushions is the
questions.why: The ostium primum is the gap below the advancing septum primum; it closes as the septum reaches the cushions.

questions.stem: Before the ostium primum closes, perforations in the septum primum form the
questions.why: Breakdown in the upper septum primum creates the ostium secundum, keeping a right-to-left path open.

questions.stem: The septum secundum differs from the septum primum in that it is

options.label: C
options.text: the floor of the coronary sinus

questions.why: The rigid septum secundum overlaps the free edge of the flap-like septum primum, converting ostium secundum into the oblique foramen ovale.

questions.stem: In the fetus the septum primum acts at the foramen ovale as a

options.label: E
options.text: flap valve allowing only right-to-left flow

questions.why: The septum primum is a flap valve permitting right-to-left atrial shunting in the fetus but not the reverse.

questions.stem: The crista terminalis of the adult right atrium is the persistent
questions.why: Fused venous valves form the septum spurium, persisting as the crista terminalis between smooth and rough right atrium.

questions.stem: Absorption of the right horn of the sinus venosus forms the
questions.why: The right sinus horn is absorbed into the smooth sinus venarum; the diminished left horn becomes the coronary sinus.

questions.stem: The coronary sinus develops from the

options.label: C
options.text: left horn of the sinus venosus

options.label: D
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: The small left sinus horn becomes the coronary sinus, opening below the sinoatrial orifice.

questions.stem: The smooth part of the left atrium is formed by absorption of the

options.label: E
options.text: right horn of the sinus venosus

questions.why: A single pulmonary vein with four branches is absorbed into the left atrial wall, forming its smooth part; trabeculated tissue becomes the auricle.

questions.stem: The lower edge of the septum secundum seen in the right atrium becomes the
questions.why: The crista dividens (lower septum secundum edge) becomes the annulus ovalis, the rim of the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: A secundum-type atrial septal defect may arise from excessive resorption of the septum primum or

options.label: B
options.text: failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse

questions.why: Secundum ASD results from too much septum-primum resorption or a septum secundum that cannot cover the ostium secundum, leaving a patent foramen ovale.

questions.stem: The muscular part of the definitive interventricular septum develops from the
questions.why: The muscular IV septum comes from the primary interventricular septum; the membranous part comes from endocardial cushions and bulbar ridges.

questions.stem: The membranous part of the interventricular septum is formed by the endocardial cushions and the
questions.why: Membranous IV septum closure is by the fused endocardial cushions and the proximal truncoconal (bulbar/conus) ridges.

questions.stem: Partitioning of the outflow tract (truncus arteriosus and conus cordis) into aorta and pulmonary trunk is achieved by a spiral septum derived from
questions.why: Neural-crest-derived truncoconal (bulbar) ridges form the spiral aorticopulmonary septum.

questions.stem: Failure of the truncoconal swellings to grow at all, leaving a single outflow vessel over a VSD, is
questions.why: Persistent truncus arteriosus is a single artery arising from both ventricles above a VSD, mixing pulmonary and systemic blood.

questions.stem: Transposition of the great arteries results from the truncoconal swellings failing to
questions.why: Non-spiral (straight) outflow septation gives TGA, with aorta from the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk from the left.

questions.stem: Tetralogy of Fallot arises from a single error in which the conus septum develops
questions.why: An anteriorly displaced conus septum yields a large overriding aorta, stenotic pulmonary trunk, VSD and right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A heart that loops to the right as a mirror image, with its apex pointing right, is
questions.why: Dextrocardia (reversed looping) points the apex to the right, often with situs inversus of all organs.

questions.stem: A heart lying partly or wholly outside the thorax, from failure of the sternum to develop, is
questions.why: Ectopia cordis is an externally located heart due to failed sternal fusion.

questions.stem: In the fetus, the vessel carrying the most oxygen-rich blood (about 80% saturation) is the
questions.why: The umbilical vein carries the highest-oxygen blood (~80%) from the placenta; the umbilical arteries carry the most deoxygenated.

questions.stem: The ductus venosus shunts oxygen-rich umbilical-vein blood directly into the
questions.why: The ductus venosus is a high-velocity shunt from the umbilical vein to the IVC, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

questions.stem: Oxygen-rich IVC blood is preferentially streamed across the foramen ovale to the left atrium by the
questions.why: The crista dividens (lower septum secundum) and IVC valve direct the oxygenated IVC stream through the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: In utero the ductus arteriosus carries approximately what proportion of right-ventricular output to the descending aorta?
questions.why: About 80-90% of RV output bypasses the high-resistance lungs via the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta.

questions.stem: The nerve that loops posteriorly around the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum is the
questions.why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta around the ductus arteriosus/ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: After birth the ductus arteriosus normally closes within
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus constricts and closes within 24-48 hours, becoming the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.stem: Closure of the ductus venosus after birth is promoted by

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in prostaglandins after cord clamping

options.label: C
options.text: the first breath inflating the lungs

questions.why: Cord clamping and a decrease in prostaglandins close the ductus venosus, which becomes the ligamentum venosum.

questions.stem: At birth the foramen ovale closes because
questions.why: Lung inflation drops right atrial pressure and raises left atrial pressure, pushing the septum primum shut against the septum secundum (later the fossa ovalis).

questions.stem: After birth, the ductus venosus becomes the
questions.why: The obliterated ductus venosus persists as the ligamentum venosum; the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
